lead: A classifier names one object in an already-cropped image. Detection asks what objects are in the full picture and where. The answer is a list of bounding boxes, each with a class label and a score. One family of models made this practical: propose a few hundred candidate boxes, run a CNN over them, keep the best after suppression. R-CNN, Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN are three steps of one idea, each removing one bottleneck of the step before. They sit behind face unlock and toll-gate number plates.
prereq: You need: 6.3 for backbone CNNs and feature maps, and Unit 5, Histogram of oriented gradients (HOG), for the descriptor style that selective search builds on.

blocks.text: A detector outputs a list. Each item is a bounding box, a class name and a score between 0 and 1. A box is written (x, y, w, h) — top-left corner in pixels, width and height in pixels — or (x₁, y₁, x₂, y₂) — top-left and bottom-right corners. The ground-truth box is the one a human drew around the object.
To score a prediction we need a number saying how well it overlaps the ground truth. That number is intersection over union.

blocks.where: B_p is the predicted box and B_g the ground-truth box, both in pixels; B_p ∩ B_g is the overlap and B_p ∪ B_g the region covered by either box; area is in px². IoU is 0 when the boxes do not touch and 1 when they are identical.

blocks.text: A detection counts as correct when its IoU with the ground truth is at least 0.5. Raise the threshold to 0.75 and you demand tighter boxes.
A detector proposes hundreds of overlapping boxes around one object. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) thins them down.

items: Sort the predicted boxes of one class by score, highest first.
Keep the top box and move it to the output list.
Compute the IoU of every remaining box with the kept box.
Delete each remaining box whose IoU is above the threshold, usually 0.5.
Repeat from step 2 with the survivors until none are left.

blocks.text: NMS runs once per class, after scoring. Across all classes it would delete a genuine object that overlaps another, such as a rider on a bicycle.

R-CNN (2014) made this work. Selective search, a classical region merger that joins neighbouring pixels by colour, texture, size and fill similarity, gives about 2000 class-independent proposals per image. Each is warped to 227×227 pixels and passed through AlexNet, giving a 4096-dimensional feature vector. On top sit one linear SVM per class, a linear box regressor, and NMS.

Two problems. The CNN sees 2000 overlapping crops per image, so the same pixels are convolved many times. And training has stages — fine-tune the CNN, train the SVMs, train the regressors — with features stored on disk.

Fast R-CNN removes the first. One convolution pass over the whole image gives a feature map. For each proposal, RoI pooling crops that map at the proposal's coordinates, splits the crop into a fixed 7×7 grid and takes the maximum in each cell. Every proposal becomes a fixed-size vector whatever its width and height. One network then carries two heads.
Head one is a softmax over C+1 classes: C object classes plus background. Head two gives 4 offset numbers per class, which move the proposal onto the object. Both heads share one loss.

blocks.where: L_cls is the cross-entropy log loss of the class head; L_box is the smooth L1 loss summed over the four box offsets; λ (often 1) balances the two.
x is one box offset error, in pixels or log-scale units; quadratic near zero and linear far away, so a few wild boxes do not dominate training.

blocks.text: Fast R-CNN trains in one stage and is several times faster than R-CNN. But proposals still come from selective search on the CPU, and that now takes most of the time.
Faster R-CNN (2015) removes selective search. The proposal step becomes a small network on the same feature map, the region proposal network (RPN).

The RPN slides a 3×3 window over the feature map. At every location it tests k anchor boxes. An anchor is a fixed reference box with a given scale and aspect ratio, typically 3 scales × 3 ratios = 9 anchors, from small squares to wide rectangles. For each anchor the RPN gives two objectness scores (object, background) and four offsets that move the anchor onto the object: 6k numbers per location.

Anchors get labels by IoU: above 0.7 with a ground truth is positive, below 0.3 is negative, the rest are ignored. The original paper trained in four alternating steps; later schemes train jointly in one pass.

One fix came later. RoI pooling rounds box coordinates to whole pixels, so the crop drifts from the true box by a pixel or two. RoI Align samples four points inside each grid cell with bilinear interpolation instead of rounding. The error is small for boxes and large for pixel-accurate masks, so the segmentation chapter uses it — see 6.6.

How is a detector scored? For one class, sort its detections by score and at each rank compute precision and recall. Average precision (AP) is the area under that precision-recall curve. Mean average precision (mAP) is the average of AP over all classes at a fixed IoU, usually 0.5.
One-stage detectors drop proposals and predict boxes straight from the image — see 6.5.

spec.aria: Two 80 by 100 pixel boxes offset by 20 pixels each way with their 60 by 80 overlap shaded. Text gives the union 11,200 px² and IoU 0.43. On the right, a kept box scored 0.90 and a crossed-out dashed box scored 0.85.

examples.question: A detector predicts one box (30, 40, 110, 140) for the class 'car', and the ground-truth box is (50, 60, 130, 160). Both are (x₁, y₁, x₂, y₂) in pixels. (a) Compute the IoU. (b) Two boxes of the same class score 0.90 and 0.85, with IoU 0.6 between them. The NMS threshold is 0.5. Which boxes survive?
steps: Predicted area: width 110 − 30 = 80 px, height 140 − 40 = 100 px, area 8000 px².
Ground-truth area: width 130 − 50 = 80 px, height 160 − 60 = 100 px, area 8000 px².
Overlap in x: from max(30, 50) = 50 to min(110, 130) = 110, so 60 px.
Overlap in y: from max(40, 60) = 60 to min(140, 160) = 140, so 80 px.
(b) Sort by score: 0.90 kept. Its IoU with the 0.85 box is 0.6 > 0.5, so the 0.85 box is suppressed.
examples.answer: IoU = 4800 ÷ 11,200 = 0.4286 (about 0.43), a weak match; after NMS only the 0.90 box survives, because 0.6 > 0.5 suppresses the 0.85 box.
examples.check:
x1p, y1p, x2p, y2p = 30, 40, 110, 140
x1g, y1g, x2g, y2g = 50, 60, 130, 160
area_p = (x2p - x1p) * (y2p - y1p)
area_g = (x2g - x1g) * (y2g - y1g)
iw = min(x2p, x2g) - max(x1p, x1g)
ih = min(y2p, y2g) - max(y1p, y1g)
inter = iw * ih
union = area_p + area_g - inter
print(area_p, area_g, inter, union, round(inter / union, 4))
scores = [0.90, 0.85]
kept = [scores[0]] if 0.6 > 0.5 else scores
print(kept)

traps: IoU uses areas, not centre distances. Boxes that look close on a sketch can still score 0.43.
NMS runs per class, after scoring. Suppressing across classes deletes a real object that overlaps another.
mAP is the mean of average precision over classes, not a mean of IoU values, and it is reported at a fixed IoU, usually 0.5.
Do not swap the sizes: R-CNN warps each proposal to 227×227 pixels, while Fast R-CNN pools each proposal to a 7×7 feature grid.
The class head has C+1 outputs. Forgetting background makes the softmax the wrong size.

quiz.q: Write a bounding box in both standard forms and name each term.
quiz.a: (x, y, w, h): (x, y) is the top-left corner in pixels, w and h are width and height in pixels. (x₁, y₁, x₂, y₂): top-left and bottom-right corners, all in pixels.

quiz.q: Why is R-CNN slow compared with Fast R-CNN?
quiz.a: R-CNN runs the CNN on about 2000 warped crops per image, so overlapping pixels are convolved many times, and it trains in separate stages with features on disk. Fast R-CNN convolves the image once and RoI-pools each proposal from that shared map.

quiz.q: Predicted box (0, 0, 10, 10), ground truth (5, 5, 15, 15), both in pixels. Compute the IoU.
quiz.a: Each area = 10 × 10 = 100 px². Overlap is 5 px in x and 5 px in y, so intersection = 25 px². Union = 100 + 100 − 25 = 175 px². IoU = 25 ÷ 175 = 0.143.

quiz.q: Three boxes of one class score 0.90, 0.80 and 0.70. IoU(0.90, 0.80) = 0.3 and IoU(0.90, 0.70) = 0.7. NMS threshold is 0.5. What survives?
quiz.a: Sort: 0.90 kept. 0.3 ≤ 0.5, so 0.80 is kept. 0.7 > 0.5, so 0.70 is suppressed. Survivors: the 0.90 and 0.80 boxes.

quiz.q: What does RoI pooling produce, and why is a fixed size needed?
quiz.a: It crops the feature map at a proposal's coordinates and max-pools it into a 7×7 grid, giving a fixed-size vector. The fully connected heads need a fixed input length, but proposals come in all sizes.

quiz.q: Faster R-CNN and Fast R-CNN use the same RoI head. Why is Faster R-CNN faster then?
quiz.a: Because proposals no longer come from selective search on the CPU. The RPN is a small convolutional network on the shared feature map, so proposal generation costs almost nothing extra and runs on the GPU with the rest.

quiz.q: Why are anchors needed in the RPN, and why several scales and ratios?
quiz.a: The RPN must output boxes from grid positions alone. Anchors give each position reference boxes, so the network predicts only offsets. Objects differ in size and shape, so several scales and aspect ratios are used; one shape would label most anchors negative.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pretrained Faster R-CNN with a ResNet backbone is a few lines in any deep learning library. Research moved to anchor-free heads such as FCOS and CenterNet, and to set-prediction detectors like DETR that drop anchors and NMS together. RoI Align is now the default in every RoI head. Look next at feature pyramid networks and focal loss.
